correctness.rationale: Under the conventional simple-arc bisection definition, Cañete–Segura Gomis Proposition 3.1 validly reduces arbitrary curved cuts without an equal-area constraint to a central segment. For R=[−A,A]×[−B,B], A≥B>0, a central cut hitting horizontal edges at (t,B), (−t,−B) has a piece containing (−t,−B) and (A,B), forcing squared diameter ≥(A+t)^2+4B^2≥A^2+4B^2 (reflection makes t≥0). A cut meeting vertical edges at (A,u),(−A,−u) forces squared diameter ≥4A^2+(B+u)^2≥A^2+4B^2. Equality in the first class forces t=0; in the second forces A=B and u=0. The vertical midline produces two A×2B rectangles, diameter sqrt(A²+4B²)=sqrt(L²/4+H²). For square there are exactly two orthogonal central optimum cuts. Analytic inequalities were independently algebraically expanded; no finite computation is taken as an all-parameter proof.

evidence: Cañete–Segura Gomis arXiv:1803.00321v1, Section 5, printed p.13/Figure 12 (PDF page index 12), explicitly says the standard bisection of every rectangle is minimizing. Definition 4.1, printed p.10, identifies the standard cut as two symmetric inradius segments, and Figure 8, printed p.11, shows the midpoint segment joining the two long horizontal edges. For rectangle width L and height H, this cuts two (L/2) by H rectangles; hence the precise published minimizer has objective sqrt((L/2)^2+H^2), exactly the submitted claimed optimum. The numerical closed form need not be printed to be mathematically covered.
The 2018 paper explicitly uses the word rectangle in Section 5 and Figure 12, directly contrary to the submitted source assessment that the full text contains no rectangle specialization.
The 2014 claim about then-unknown general optimum directions predates the 2018 rectangle statement, so it cannot override the later result.

originality.rationale: Decisive published prior implication: the 2018 primary paper already proves the very same midpoint cut is optimal for every rectangle, not just squares. The claimed exact value follows immediately from the Pythagorean diameter of either resultant half-rectangle. The present center-line uniqueness clause may not be stated verbatim there, but its strictness is a two-case elementary inequality and does not give an independently substantive discovery. Earlier self-review PASS and a mistaken old statement that the 2018 paper had no rectangle reference were not used.
residual_risks: It is conceivable that the strict uniqueness of the optimal center-passing line is not explicitly written in the 2018 paper; it follows from immediate strict inequalities and is not assessed as an independently valuable research gap.

evidence: arXiv:1803.00321 (2018), Definition 4.1, Figures 8/12, Section 5 explicitly verifies optimum rectangle midline.
The formula sqrt(H²+L²/4) is exactly the diagonal length of the (L/2)×H half rectangle, one step after the published result.
The equality refinements are 2At+t²>0 for t>0 and 3(A²−B²)+2Bu+u²>0 unless A=B,u=0.
limitations: An explicit strict center-line equality classification may not have been stated in 2018, but it is not independently substantive enough to rescue this claim.
No general new theorem or classification beyond the previously known optimizer is supplied.
value.rationale: The rectangle family and max-diameter invariant are natural, but the published 2018 theorem already solves the actual optimization on all rectangles: it explicitly shows that the inradius midline is minimizing (Section 5/Figure 12). Evaluating the two resulting rectangle diagonals is an immediate textbook Pythagorean calculation. The only additional detail, strict uniqueness of the center-passing direction, is two elementary positivity inequalities and is not a motivated substantial independent exact classification once the optimizer is already known. This is a failed novelty/value contribution, not a challenge to the correctness or intrinsic importance of the fencing problem.
